_source: Hand-written for habits.test.ts (no tester data). Sentences are written the way a recogniser outputs them: lowercase, no punctuation. ESL groups are patterns described in the literature and heard in everyday speech, not transcripts of real people. This is the DEV set: rules were tuned against it. habits-holdout.json was written at the same time and never tuned on.
_markup: Tokens are separated by spaces. Every habit-word occurrence carries a mark; the test fails if one is unmarked.
word/F  filler, confident     word/f  filler, needs audio or more context to be sure
word/R  real, confident       word/r  real, needs audio or more context to be sure
Two-word habits are joined: you_know/F, i_mean/r, kind_of/R, sort_of/r. kinda/sorta count as kind of/sort of.

|  marks a pause of about 700 ms. Items with a pause get steady synthetic audio times (word starts every ~300 ms, words end before the next starts). Items with "timing": "bursty" get arrival-style times instead (whole batches share one stamp), which the classifier must ignore.
Confident means: someone reading this transcript (and its pause marks, if any) would agree with the label without hearing more.
_labelling_rules: 1. REAL when the word does grammatical or semantic work a listener would miss: a verb (i like it, do you know, i mean it, let you know), a comparison, preposition or 'such as' (looks like, like a puzzle, like that, tools like jira, people like me), like = as (like i said), a degree word (so much, so good), a conjunction joining two clauses (so that, we were late so we cancelled), a pro-form or fixed phrase (i think so, or so, and so on), right as adverb or adjective (right now, the right way, you're right), kind of / sort of as a noun (a kind of tool, what sort of role), literally in its literal sense (take it literally, literally called, literally the title), actually as contrast or reality check (did it actually work, what actually happened).

2. ALSO REAL (normal speech, changes register more than meaning, and normal in many Englishes): like as an approximator before a number or amount (like fifty people, like ten minutes), quotative be like (she was like no way), a hedge (kind of slow, we sort of agreed, it's kinda late), ONE tag question (we ship friday right, it was hard you know), ONE discourse opener at the start of a turn or clause (so, actually, basically, right, all right, you know, i mean as a self-repair), a single mid-clause intensifier (i literally ran, it's basically free, i actually disagree), a sentence-final actually (it works actually), and Indian English emphatic actually/only/itself. Two discourse openers together count as one opener (so basically, right so, so actually).

3. FILLER when deleting it changes neither grammar nor meaning and it does no discourse job: like inserted inside a clause (it was like huge, the meeting like went long, and like the client said no, they like said no); like or you know or i mean or kind of next to an um/uh or stacked with another habit word (like um, um like, you know like, i mean like, kind of you know); a run of three habit words (actually like basically); stutter repeats (like like, you know you know, so so, actually actually); you know inside a noun phrase or clause (the you know budget, it was you know bad); a habit word set off by pauses inside a clause where it frames nothing (we need | like | faster builds); and the tic case: the same discourse word used 3+ times within about 15 words where each use could be deleted.
4. A discourse opener followed by a hesitation stays real (so um the numbers, actually um i wanted): the um is the filler, and align.ts already counts it.
5. When in doubt, REAL. This makes precision harder, not easier: every doubtful case the classifier calls filler is counted against it.
